step_by_step_reasoning: The analysis began by identifying the overall graph's purpose and name, 'CrazyWall', from the visual diagram and transcript. Nodes were then extracted by strictly adhering to the 'visual-first' rule, focusing on distinct icons and bounded boxes. Floating text like 'API CRAZYWALL', 'API BLOCKING', and 'Blocking' were not made into nodes but were used to inform edge notes. AWS service nodes were mapped to the exact strings from the provided list. Non-AWS components with distinct icons (Pi Event Processor, Ticketing System, Neptune ML) were categorized as 'ThirdParty' as they are either custom systems or not explicitly in the AWS service list. Edges were drawn based on visible arrows on the whiteboard. Logical flow IDs and sequential `seq` values were assigned, starting with data ingestion and progressing through real-time processing, decision making, API interactions, and future ML integration. Special attention was paid to the constraint of not creating speculative return paths unless explicitly drawn, and only using services from the provided list. The '90%' and '35K' labels were treated as explanatory text or metrics related to specific processes (BeanStalk's precision, blocked users count) and not distinct nodes or direct edge labels in a way that would require new nodes.

graph.name: CrazyWall
graph.categories: Fraud Detection, Graph Database, Real-time Processing, Historical Data Processing
graph.notes: Karim's 'CrazyWall' fraud detection system integrates historical user data with real-time event processing. Historical data from S3 is processed via EMR and loaded into Neptune, a graph database representing user identities and relationships. Real-time user events are captured by a custom 'Pi Event Processor', streamed through SQS, and processed by Elastic Beanstalk. Beanstalk writes processed data to Neptune and performs rule-based fraud detection. Fraud decisions are stored in RDS, with high-value cases routed to a 'Ticketing System' for manual review. The system also exposes an API for other teams and a blocking API. Future plans involve integrating Neptune ML for enhanced prediction accuracy.

nodes.name: S3
nodes.notes: Hosts the data warehouse with historical user data.

nodes.name: EMR
nodes.notes: Extracts and processes historical data from S3 using PySpark ETL, transforming it for Neptune.

nodes.name: Neptune
nodes.notes: Graph database storing historical and real-time user identities, data points, and relationships for fraud detection. Used for both initial data load and real-time lookups.

nodes.name: Pi Event Processor
nodes.notes: Custom system developed by Kareem engineers to process every user event (login, ride, purchase) on the app in real-time.

nodes.name: SQS
nodes.notes: Queue for streaming real-time events from the Pi Event Processor to Elastic Beanstalk.

nodes.name: Elastic Beanstalk
nodes.notes: Core codebase that processes and transforms real-time event data, writes to Neptune, performs rule-based fraud detection, and provides APIs for graph queries and blocking.

nodes.name: Users
nodes.notes: Represents end-users interacting with the Karim application, performing actions that generate events.

nodes.name: UI
nodes.notes: Internal user interface used by Kareem teams to query and view user identity details in the graph via an API.

nodes.name: RDS
nodes.notes: Stores fraud classification decisions made by the Elastic Beanstalk application.

nodes.name: Ticketing System
nodes.notes: An external ticketing system for manual review of high-value customers classified as potentially fraudulent.

nodes.name: Neptune ML
nodes.notes: Future integration (version 2) for training deep learning models (graph convolutional network) on the Neptune graph to improve fraud prediction accuracy, replacing the rule-based system in Elastic Beanstalk.

edges.notes: Historical data is extracted from S3 by EMR.
EMR runs an ETL pipeline using PySpark to load transformed historical data into the Neptune graph database.
User actions on the application generate real-time events processed by the Pi Event Processor.
Real-time user events are streamed from the Pi Event Processor into an SQS queue.
The Elastic Beanstalk core codebase consumes events from the SQS queue.
Processed and transformed real-time event data is written to the Neptune graph database.
After an event, Elastic Beanstalk performs a second read to extract user data and surrounding neighbors from Neptune for fraud analysis.
Fraud classification decisions from Elastic Beanstalk's rule-based system are written to RDS.
Decisions for high-value customers identified as potentially fraudulent are sent to a ticketing system for manual review.
Elastic Beanstalk exposes a 'CrazyWall' API allowing users/downstream tasks to query graph data about user identities.
Elastic Beanstalk exposes a 'CrazyWall' API allowing internal UIs to query graph data about user identities.
Elastic Beanstalk provides a 'Blocking' API that interacts with RDS to manage fraud decisions and user blocking (for lower value users, automatically blocked).
Neptune ML trains deep learning models using data from the Neptune graph database.
Neptune ML's predictions or trained models will be used by Elastic Beanstalk to enhance fraud detection accuracy.
